problems.title: What did you time?
problems.statement: Host code: t0 = now(); launch(k); t1 = now(); with no synchronisation. The kernel runs for 2 ms; issuing a launch costs 5 µs.

options: Synchronise (or record events) before reading the clock

problems.solution: About 5 µs: the cost of queuing the launch. Synchronise before t1, or better, record CUDA events on the stream around the kernel.

problems.title: Summarising runs
hints: The first run includes loading the kernel.
problems.solution: Mean 24.38 (dragged up by the cold first run and one interrupted run), median 8.50, minimum 8.4. Report the median (typical) or minimum (best case) after discarding warm-up, and say which.

problems.title: Latency versus throughput
problems.statement: A tiny kernel runs for 3 µs on the GPU; launch overhead is 5 µs per launch.

parts.prompt: Time per kernel when launched and synchronised one at a time, in µs?
Time per kernel for 1,000 back-to-back launches with one final sync, in µs?

options: idle 40% of the time, waiting for launches

hints: Back to back, the host issues while the GPU runs the previous kernel: the slower of the two sets the pace.
problems.solution: (a) 5 + 3 = 8 µs. (b) The host can only issue one launch per 5 µs, so the GPU finishes each 3-µs kernel and waits: 5 µs per kernel, the GPU idle 2/5 of the time. That's launch-bound; CUDA Graphs or fusion fix it.

problems.title: Is the difference real?
problems.statement: Version A: median 10.0 µs, runs spread from 9.6 to 10.6. Version B: median 9.7 µs, spread from 9.3 to 10.4. Both measured interleaved, 50 runs each.

parts.prompt: Can you claim B is 3% faster?
options: Not from these numbers alone: the spreads overlap heavily; you need more runs or a statistical test

hints: Compare the difference with the spread.
problems.solution: A 0.3 µs difference inside a 1 µs spread: possibly real, not established. Report the distributions, or run a rank test (e.g. Mann–Whitney) on the interleaved samples. Many published "speedups" don't survive this.

problems.title: Why interleave?
problems.statement: The GPU warms up over the benchmark, so the clock rises by 5% during the first half of the session and then stays put. You run 50 of A, then 50 of B.

options: B looks faster than it is, because it ran on a warmer, faster clock

parts.prompt: Apparent speedup of B, in %, if A and B are actually identical and A's runs averaged 2.5% slower clocks?

hints: Drift hits whichever version runs later.
problems.solution: B ran entirely at the higher clock: an apparent ~2.5% gain that is pure drift. Interleaving (A, B, A, B, …) exposes both to the same conditions. Locking clocks (Chapter 9.3) removes the drift entirely.

problems.title: The first run
problems.statement: Why is the first launch of a kernel slow?

options: The kernel's code is loaded onto the device (or JIT-compiled from PTX)
The GPU's clock ramps up from idle
Memory allocations made earlier are lazily committed

problems.solution: Module loading (or JIT), clock ramp, cold caches and lazily mapped memory all hit the first iteration. Hence warm-up runs. The GPU doesn't reboot.

problems.title: Events versus host timers
problems.statement: A kernel runs 40 µs. Host timer with synchronise: 52 µs. CUDA events around the launch: 40.5 µs.

parts.prompt: Overhead included by the host-timer method, in µs?

hints: Events are timestamped on the GPU, in stream order.
problems.solution: 12 µs of launch and synchronisation overhead. Events measure GPU time between two points in the stream: the kernel. The host timer measures what a caller waits, which is right for end-to-end latency, wrong for kernel speed.

problems.title: Copying hides the bug
problems.statement: t0; launch; cudaMemcpy(result back); t1 with no explicit synchronise.

parts.prompt: Does t1 − t0 include the kernel?
options: Yes: the copy waits for the kernel (same stream), so the time includes kernel + copy

parts.prompt: Kernel 2 ms, copy of 64 MB over 25 GB/s PCIe: measured time, in ms?

problems.solution: Yes: the blocking copy waits for the kernel, so the number is kernel + copy = 4.56 ms. It looks like a kernel timing but isn't one.

problems.title: Throughput of a pipeline
problems.statement: 1,000 kernels each running 20 µs on the GPU, launch overhead 5 µs, launched back to back.

options: No: the GPU never waits, since each kernel takes longer than issuing the next

problems.solution: The host queues launches faster than the GPU drains them, so the GPU runs continuously: about 20 ms + the first launch's 5 µs. Launch overhead only matters when kernels are shorter than it.

problems.title: What to report

parts.prompt: Which belong in an honest report?
options: GPU model, driver, clocks or clock policy

problems.solution: Everything needed to reproduce and judge it. An unlabelled best run is cherry-picking.
